concepts.objective: Specify a treatment, comparison, population and outcome, and distinguish setting a treatment from observing its value.
Calculate a population-average contrast between two intervention values, stating direction, units and target population without assigning it to each individual.
Explain confounding and standardize stratum-specific outcomes to a common population only under an adequate pre-treatment adjustment set, overlap and consistency.
Distinguish effect identification under explicit causal and design assumptions from estimation with finite data and from generalization to another population.

claims.proposition: An intervention replaces the assignment mechanism of the selected variable; observing a value generally leaves its causes and selection process in place.

source_refs.locator: Sections 3.2 and 6.3, intervention definitions and Example 6.10

claims.proposition: An average causal effect contrasts expected outcomes under two specified interventions in a specified population; for a binary outcome a risk difference is expressed in probability or percentage points.

A valid adjustment formula combines conditional outcome distributions with the same pre-intervention covariate distribution for each treatment. Validity depends on the causal structure, not merely on including many variables.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.6, Definition 6.38, equations (6.13)-(6.15), and the warning following Definition 6.39

claims.proposition: An intervention distribution may be determined by observational data together with a causal model and valid adjustment assumptions; an observational association alone need not determine it.

claims.proposition: Reference counts and assessment cases in this pack are authored teaching data. Interactive experiment outcomes are deterministically recomputed from the released model and learner settings. Ratios, differences and weighted sums use declared denominators and target weights. Generation fidelity and withholding criteria are declared teaching-model rules, not empirical guarantees or textbook claims about a particular generator.

resources.text: For eligible rehabilitation patients, compare assignment to programme A with assignment to programme B. Success means reach the mobility target at six weeks; choosing a programme is not the same as being assigned one.
Worked example

For eligible rehabilitation patients, let A=1 mean assignment to the specified six-week programme and A=0 mean assignment to its stated comparison. Define success and the follow-up time. The notation do(A=1) means actively setting assignment to 1, not selecting existing records with A=1.

People choosing a programme may differ in motivation, access or baseline mobility limitation. Those factors can also affect success. Filtering existing programme users leaves that selection process in place.

Randomizing the offer can support an effect of being offered the programme under the study conditions. If some people do not use the offer, the effect of actual use is a different question. A new programme version or population also needs separate support.

An intervention actively sets a treatment rather than selects people who already received it. Specify the treatment, alternative, target population, outcome and follow-up. Assignment and actual use can be different variables.
A historical or before-and-after comparison does not automatically reproduce random assignment; time and the people included may also differ.
Name the assigned change, its alternative, the people and the outcome time.
Random assignment changes how the specified reminder is allocated. The other plans compare existing choices or different time periods; they do not replace the assignment rule.
Check what the plan actively sets. Selecting existing users, or comparing years, leaves their original assignment process in place.
Look for an action that sets assignment, rather than a new way to group existing users.
A clinic records patients who enabled appointment reminders themselves. Which plan actively changes reminder assignment?
Random assignment changes how the specified reminder is allocated. The other plans compare existing choices or different time periods; they do not replace the assignment rule.
The study randomizes the offer, not uptake. Selective uptake can make an actual-use comparison different; future policies and populations define further targets.
Distinguish the assigned offer from later uptake and from a new policy. The study design directly supports only its specified assignment comparison.
Identify the variable randomized before considering what people later chose to use.
A hospital randomly offers transport support; some offered patients do not use it. Attendance is measured over 30 days. Which effect does the randomized comparison target?
The study randomizes the offer, not uptake. Selective uptake can make an actual-use comparison different; future policies and populations define further targets.
Suppose the same target population would average 68 mobility-score points under A and 62 under B. A minus B is a population-average contrast, not a promise about every person.
Worked example
Define the mean outcome if the same target population were assigned A and if it were assigned B. This is different from comparing whichever people happened to choose each programme.
For the score example, 68 - 62 = +6 mobility-score points. For a binary outcome, 75% - 60% = +15 percentage points. The relative increase is 15/60 = 25%; these are different summaries.

People can benefit by different amounts, not benefit, or be harmed while the average is positive. A finite study estimates the population contrast with uncertainty. Subtracting sample means does not remove that uncertainty.

An average treatment effect compares mean outcomes under two interventions for the same target population. Subtract the comparison from the treatment and state the units. For a binary (yes/no) outcome, a probability difference uses percentage points, not a relative percentage. Sampling uncertainty means another sample could give a different estimate.
A percentage-point difference is not a relative percentage, and an average does not identify each person's response.
Report A minus B, its units, the target population and the follow-up.
68 - 62 = +6 mobility-score points for this study population and six-week outcome. The calculation is an average score difference, not a relative percentage or an individual effect.
Keep score points separate from a relative percentage and an individual outcome. Recheck the subtraction on the stated scale.
Subtract the means on the stated scale; distinguish an average from each person's response.
Eligible participants are randomly assigned A or B. Mean six-week scores are 68 and 62 mobility-score points, respectively. Ignoring sampling uncertainty for this calculation, what is A minus B?
68 - 62 = +6 mobility-score points for this study population and six-week outcome. The calculation is an average score difference, not a relative percentage or an individual effect.
0.54 - 0.40 = 0.14, or 14 percentage points. Relative to B, the increase is 0.14/0.40 = 35%. These group outcomes do not identify individual responses; a finite study also has uncertainty.
This answer changes the quantity being reported or attributes outcomes to named individuals. Use the same denominators and distinguish group probabilities from individual effects.
A risk difference subtracts probabilities. A relative increase divides their difference by the comparison probability.
A randomized dataset reports recovery by day 30 in 54/100 assigned A and 40/100 assigned B. What is the risk difference (A minus B) for this study population?
0.54 - 0.40 = 0.14, or 14 percentage points. Relative to B, the increase is 0.14/0.40 = 35%. These group outcomes do not identify individual responses; a finite study also has uncertainty.
Baseline mobility limitation can influence both programme choice and later success. The overall A and B groups may therefore contain different starting conditions.
Worked example

If baseline mobility limitation affects choice and success, pooling all A records and all B records can mix programme differences with differences in who chose each programme. A stratum is a group with the same specified baseline category.

In a separate worked example, A/B success rates are 80%/70% in the lower-baseline group and 50%/40% in the higher-baseline group. With a half-and-half target, A is 0.5 x 80% + 0.5 x 50% = 65%; B is 55%. The contrast is +10 percentage points.

The pre-treatment variables must remove confounding; both treatments must occur in each relevant group; treatment versions must be consistent. Do not add every predictor. A mediator carries part of the treatment's effect; adjusting for it can remove that part. A collider is a common effect; conditioning on it can introduce bias.

Baseline means measured before treatment. Confounding occurs when a common cause affects treatment and outcome. Standardization compares rates within pre-treatment groups using the same target weights for both treatments; pooling keeps each selected group's own mixture. Causal interpretation requires no remaining confounding, overlap (both treatments possible) and consistency (well-defined treatment versions).
Weighting does not repair an omitted common cause or a group with no comparison treatment. A good outcome predictor is not automatically safe to adjust for.
Justify the baseline groups and use one target mixture for both alternatives.

Use each treatment's outcome rates within the adequate pre-treatment groups and a common target mixture. This has a causal interpretation under adequate adjustment, overlap and consistency, not simply because weights were calculated.
Different selected-group weights compare different mixtures. Adding more predictors is not a substitute for checking the causal assumptions.
Both treatment alternatives must describe the same target population, under the stated adjustment assumptions.

Baseline severity affects treatment choice and recovery. Assume it removes all confounding, both treatments occur at each severity, and versions are consistent. How should the target-population comparison be calculated?

Use each treatment's outcome rates within the adequate pre-treatment groups and a common target mixture. This has a causal interpretation under adequate adjustment, overlap and consistency, not simply because weights were calculated.

In the supplied model, the later variable is a mediator: it carries part of the treatment's effect. Conditioning on it can block that part. This does not invalidate the stated adequate baseline set or make observational inference impossible.
Prediction alone does not decide adjustment. Check what effect is being targeted and whether the added variable carries part of that effect.
A mediator carries an effect from treatment to outcome. Check whether the proposed variable lies on that route.

The goal is the total effect of operation type on recovery. Baseline risk already controls confounding. In the proposed model, operation type affects infection, which affects recovery. Should infection be added just because it predicts recovery?

In the supplied model, the later variable is a mediator: it carries part of the treatment's effect. Conditioning on it can block that part. This does not invalidate the stated adequate baseline set or make observational inference impossible.
A large registry can describe a group difference precisely while leaving its cause unresolved. A trial result can also be specific to the people, programme and follow-up studied.
Worked example

An effect is identified relative to a set of data and assumptions if every causal model compatible with them gives the same effect. Different models fitting the observations can otherwise imply different intervention effects.

Adjustment by baseline mobility limitation assumes no remaining confounding, both programmes possible in the relevant groups, and consistent versions. Random assignment can support an assignment-effect argument under its design and follow-up conditions. More records can reduce sampling error without repairing missing causal assumptions.

A different population, programme version or outcome time is a different target. Assess the evidence and assumptions for that target separately. Agreement between an adjusted estimate and a trial estimate does not prove every assumption, and missing follow-up can create another problem.

Identification asks whether the data and stated causal assumptions determine an effect. Estimation calculates it from a finite sample, with uncertainty. Transport asks whether it applies to another population or treatment version. A precise estimate alone does not settle the other questions.
A narrow uncertainty interval is not proof that confounding is absent or that the effect transfers to a different setting.
State why the effect is identifiable, how uncertain its estimate is, and where it applies.
A large sample can reduce sampling error for the observed association. It does not choose among intervention effects left compatible by unresolved confounding and the supplied design.
Precision and identification are different. Ask what assumption or design addresses the missing common cause, rather than how many rows are available.
More data can improve precision without deciding between different causal explanations.
A registry has a million treatment and recovery records, but a missing factor may cause both. No other identification design is supplied. What does the large sample establish?
A large sample can reduce sampling error for the observed association. It does not choose among intervention effects left compatible by unresolved confounding and the supplied design.
The trial supports its specified assignment contrast under its design conditions. Transport to different people, versions or follow-up times requires a separate argument and often more evidence.
The original design does not automatically cover a different target. Separate the study's result from the proposed extension.
Compare the proposed use with the population, treatment and follow-up actually studied.

A well-run randomized trial identifies an assignment effect for eligible adults with complete follow-up. A team applies it to children receiving a different dose and assessed later. What needs further support?
The trial supports its specified assignment contrast under its design conditions. Transport to different people, versions or follow-up times requires a separate argument and often more evidence.

Pooling retains the composition of each selected programme group. Standardization applies common target weights. Its causal meaning still requires adequate pre-treatment adjustment, overlap and consistency; use saved runs for computed values.
A pooled rate can mix outcome differences with group composition. A weighted result still depends on the causal assumptions; weighting alone does not verify them.
Compare which baseline mixture contributes to each programme's average in the two analyses.
